metadata.title: McMillian v. Monroe County, 520 U.S. 781 (1997) (No. 96-542)
metadata.creator: Supreme Court of the United States
metadata.description:
Case name: McMillian v. Monroe County

Opinion filed: 1997-06-02

Docket No.: 96-542

Citations:
• 138 L. Ed. 2d 1
• 117 S. Ct. 1734
• 520 U.S. 781
• 1997 U.S. LEXIS 3398

Case holding summaries:
• noting that official need only have final policy-making authority in "a particular area[ ] or on a particular issue" of municipal business to be final policymaker
• “Alabama sheriffs, when executing their law enforcement duties, represent the State of Alabama . . . .”
• finding that “Alabama sheriffs, when executing their law enforcement duties, represent the State of Alabama, not their counties”
• finding this designation "especially important" for determining liability
• establishing an analytical framework for determining whether a state actor is acting on behalf of the state, and thus entitled to Eleventh Amendment immunity, or a county or local municipality, and thus not so entitled
• applying Pembaur's principles in a suit against the county
• relying on the “the constitutional provisions concerning sheriffs, the historical development of those provisions, and the interpretation given them by the Alabama Supreme Court” to determine whether Alabama sheriffs represent the State for purposes of liability under 42 U.S.C. § 1983
• applying Monell's principles to a suit against a county
• applying Monell 's principles to a suit against a county
• applying Pembaur 's principles in a suit against the county
• "The county's payment of the sheriff's salary does not translate into control over [the sheriff], since the county neither has the authority to change [the sheriff's] salary nor the discretion to refuse payment completely."
• holding that for purposes of applying 42 U.S.C. § 1983, Alabama sheriffs, when executing their law enforcement duties, represent the State of Alabama rather than their counties
• determining that a County is liable, under Section 1983, for the actions of its Sheriff which constitute County policy
• establishing an analytical framework for determining whether a state actor is acting on behalf of the state, and thus entitled to Eleventh Amendment immunity, or a county or local municipality, and thus not so entitled
• holding that a county sheriff was a state official for purposes of Section 1983
• "The county's payment of the sheriff's salary does not translate into control over [the sheriff], since the county neither has the authority to change his salary nor the discretion to refuse payment completely."
• concluding that Alabama sheriffs act for the state as to the law enforcement function in issue
• requiring analysis of the "particular area" at issue and contrasting it with a "categorical, `all or nothing'" approach
• finding that "Alabama sheriffs, when executing their law enforcement duties, represent the State of Alabama, not their counties"
• noting that a suit against a governmental officer in his official capacity is the same as a suit against the entity of which the officer is an agent
• “[O]ur understanding of the actual function of a governmental official, in a particular area, will necessarily be dependent on the definition of the official’s functions under relevant state law.”
• Maryland sheriff sets county policy in area of jail conditions, based on exhaustive survey of Maryland law; citing no constitutional provision to the contrary
• Arkansas sheriff sets county policy in area of law enforcement; citing no constitutional provision to the contrary
• Wisconsin sheriff acts on behalf of State, not county, in hiring and firing employees
• state law granting immunity to parole officers does not control question whether such officers have immunity under § 1983
• Illinois sheriff does not set county policy in area of training jail employees, because county board of commissioners has no authority to set policy in this area
• Florida sheriff acts for county in hiring and firing deputies
• sheriffs are county officers for purposes of 1912 constitutional amendment regarding county officers' salaries
• sheriff elected by residents of county to be county's chief law enforcement officer, paid and equipped by county, is "obvious[ly]" a county official
• Alabama sheriff acts for county in hiring chief jailor
• courts of appeals review de novo district courts' state-law determinations
• county may reasonably limit budget for overtime pay for sheriff's deputies
• "We generally accord great deference to the interpretation and application of state law by the courts of appeals"
• Massachusetts sheriff acts for county in setting county jail strip search policy
• Michigan sheriff acts for county in training deputies and ratifying deputies' use of force
• Texas sheriff sets county policy in area of law enforcement, based on "unique structure of county government in Texas"; citing no constitutional provision to the contrary (internal quotation marks omitted)
• "We think the Court of Appeals [for the Fifth Circuit], whose expertise in interpreting Texas law is greater than our own, is in a better position to determine whether [the school district superintendent] possessed final policymaking authority in the area of employee transfers"
• Washington sheriff sets county policy in area of training deputy sheriffs, based on statutory provision labeling sheriff "chief executive officer . . . of the county"; citing no constitutional provision to the contrary (internal quotation marks omitted)
• New York sheriff acts for county in setting county jail strip search policy
• "We are not, of course, predicting that state law will always speak with perfect clarity"
• "It may not be possible to draw an elegant line that will resolve this conundrum"
• "The States have extremely wide latitude in determining the form that local government takes . . . . [O]ne may expect to find a rich variety of ways in which the power of government is distributed among a host of different officials and official bodies."
• Virginia "city sheriff" does not set city policy in area of jail conditions
• defenses to § 1983 actions are questions of federal law
• "[The] federal question can be answered only after considering the provisions of state law that define the agency's character"
• noting that a suit against a governmental officer in his official capacity is the same as a suit against the entity of which the officer is an agent
• courts must determine whether officials are policymakers for the municipality “in a particular area, or on a particular issue”
• discussing why state policymakers' actions do not lead to municipal liability
• noting that one of the historical functions of officers is to pre- serve the public peace
• “[T]he salaries of all sheriffs are set by the state legislature, not by the county commissions.”
